comparisons.peer_topic: Net Charge-Offs and Provision for Credit Losses Drivers
comparisons.peer_summary: Net charge-offs for 2024 were $6.0 billion, up from $3.8 billion in 2023, primarily due to credit card loans and the commercial real estate office portfolio. The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion, driven by credit card and small business loan growth and asset quality deterioration in commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC) report significant increases in provision for credit losses and net charge-offs for 2024, driven primarily by their credit card portfolios. JPM reported a $10.7 billion provision with $8.6 billion in net charge-offs, specifically noting that the increase in net charge-offs was 'driven by Card Services' due to 'seasoning of vintages,' 'credit normalization,' and 'balance growth.' Similarly, BAC reported a $5.8 billion provision with $6.0 billion in net charge-offs, stating the increase from the prior year was 'primarily due to credit card loans' and listing 'credit card... portfolios' as primary drivers of the provision. Both firms attribute the deterioration to card-specific factors, though JPM highlights the maturation/seasoning of loans while BAC also cites commercial real estate office deterioration as a concurrent factor.

sentences.text: • The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion of net charge-offs and a net addition to the allowance for credit losses of $2.0 billion. Net charge-offs increased by $2.4 billion, driven by Card Services, reflecting the seasoning of vintages originated in recent years, credit normalization, and balance growth. The net addition to the allowance for credit losses included a net addition of $2.1 billion in consumer, driven by Card Services, and a net reduction of $19 million in wholesale.
Net charge-offs for 2024 were $6.0 billion compared to $3.8 billion in 2023 primarily due to credit card loans and the commercial real estate office portfolio.

The provision for credit losses in 2024 was primarily driven by credit card as well as small business loan growth, and asset quality deterioration in the commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provisions were $8.6 billion, up from $6.7 billion, largely driven by a 45% increase in net credit losses to $7.6 billion, reflecting the maturation of card loan vintages, macroeconomic pressures from inflation and interest rates, and impacts on lower FICO band customers, with Branded Cards and Retail Services losses rising 51% and 39% respectively.
comparisons.comparison: Capital One (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) both report 2024 provisions for credit losses largely driven by net credit losses in their card businesses, with explicit references to the maturation or seasoning of loan vintages. JPM reported a $10.7 billion provision with $8.6 billion in net charge-offs, attributing the rise to 'Card Services' and the 'seasoning of vintages originated in recent years.' Capital One reported a higher provision of $8.6 billion against $7.6 billion in net credit losses, stating this was 'largely driven by higher net credit losses' which primarily reflected the 'continued maturation of multiple cards loan vintages originated in recent years.' Both disclosures identify the aging/seasoning of recently originated card portfolios as a core driver of the 2024 loss rates.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion in 2024 from $1.14 billion in 2023, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio.

Both disclosures center the credit loss narrative on the performance and charge-off behavior of their respective credit card assets.
